title: Design a rate limiter
scopeHtml: Scope: token bucket, sliding window, Redis Lua atomicity, distributed limiting, API and headers, failure modes.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A rate limiter caps how many requests a client may make in a time window, and rejects the extra ones. It protects services from abuse, bugs (a client retry loop) and overload, and enforces plans ("free tier: 100 requests/min"). Stripe, GitHub, Twitter and Cloudflare all publish limits.

Functional

  • Limit by key: user ID, API key, IP, or endpoint (for example POST /login stricter than GET /feed).
  • Return a clear rejection and tell the client when to retry.
  • Rules configurable without a deploy.

Non-functional

  • Adds under 2 ms to each request (it is in the hot path).
  • Works across many app servers (a distributed counter, not per-server).
  • Highly available: if the limiter breaks, the product should not go down (decide fail-open vs fail-closed).
  • Reasonably accurate; small over-allowance is acceptable.

Decision gravity. Where to put the limiter: in the gateway (one place, easy, reversible), in each service (flexible, duplicated), or in a client SDK (cannot be trusted). Gateway is the standard choice. Moving it later is cheap, but the choice of algorithm affects client-visible behaviour, so changing it can surprise customers.

Everyday analogy. A bouncer at a club counting how many people entered in the last minute.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to ask: per user, per IP, or per endpoint? hard or soft limit?
  • Designing a single-server limiter and ignoring distribution.
  • Not deciding fail-open vs fail-closed.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
The limiter is mostly internal, but the client-facing contract matters.

Response headers on every call (de-facto GitHub/Stripe style, IETF draft RateLimit-*):

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-RateLimit-Limit: 100
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 37
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1731150060        (unix time window resets)
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 12
Content-Type: application/json
{ "error": "rate_limited", "retryAfterSeconds": 12 }

Internal check API (gateway to limiter service, or a library call):

POST /internal/check
{ "key": "user:42", "rule": "api-default", "cost": 1 }
200 { "allowed": true, "remaining": 37, "resetMs": 12000 }
200 { "allowed": false, "remaining": 0, "retryAfterMs": 12000 }

Rules config (hot-reloaded from a config store):

rules:
  - id: api-default
    key: user_id
    limit: 100
    window: 60s
    algorithm: token_bucket
    burst: 20
  - id: login
    key: ip
    limit: 5
    window: 60s

Industry example. Stripe returns 429 and recommends exponential backoff; GitHub documents X-RateLimit-* headers and 5,000 requests/hour for authenticated calls.

Everyday analogy. The sign on the club door showing "capacity 100, inside now 63".

Common interview traps.

  • Returning 403 or 500 instead of 429.
  • Omitting Retry-After, so clients retry immediately and make it worse.
  • Not including a cost for expensive calls.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 500M requests/day to the API.

Quantity Calculation Result
Average QPS 500M / 86,400 about 5,800/s
Peak QPS 3x about 17,000/s
Active keys 10M users in a minute 10M
Memory per key (token bucket) key 20 B + tokens 8 B + timestamp 8 B + overhead ~64 B ~100 B
Total memory 10M x 100 B ~1 GB
Sliding-log memory (100 req/min) 10M x 100 timestamps x 8 B ~8 GB (much worse)

17,000 checks/s is small for one Redis node (100k+ simple ops/s). Memory is the lever that picks the algorithm: counters and buckets are tiny, per-request logs are not.

Everyday analogy. Counting people with a clicker (one number) versus writing a name for each person (a long list).

Common interview traps.

  • Picking sliding log without computing memory at scale.
  • Ignoring that each check is a network hop (budget 1 ms).

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Flow

  1. Request arrives; middleware builds the key (for example rl:user:42:api-default).
  2. It runs one atomic operation in Redis (Lua script) that refills, checks and decrements.
  3. Allowed: forward and add headers. Denied: return 429 with Retry-After.
  4. Rules are cached locally and refreshed from a config service every 30 s.

Why Redis. In-memory, single-threaded atomic scripts, TTL for auto cleanup, Cluster for sharding by key. Alternatives: Memcached (no scripts, but incr works for fixed window), a local in-process limiter (no shared state, loses accuracy across N servers), or a dedicated service (adds a network hop but centralises logic).

Decision gravity. A central store gives accurate global limits but a new dependency in the hot path; local limits are fast and resilient but allow N times the limit. Many companies use both: local approximate limit first, then global. Reversible, since the algorithm sits behind a small interface.

Industry examples. Stripe describes a Redis-based token bucket; Cloudflare uses a sliding-window approximation at the edge; Envoy supports a global rate limit service (Lyft's ratelimit) plus a local token bucket.

Everyday analogy. One shared clipboard at the club door versus each doorman keeping their own count.

Common interview traps.

  • Counting per app server and calling it "global".
  • Reading then writing in two Redis calls (race condition).

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
The algorithms

  1. Fixed window counter. INCR key, EXPIRE key 60. Cheap, but a burst at a window boundary can allow 2x the limit (100 at 10:00:59 and 100 at 10:01:00).
  2. Sliding window log. Store every request timestamp in a sorted set; count those in the last 60 s. Exact, but memory heavy (see estimates).
  3. Sliding window counter. Keep the current and previous window counts and weight: prev x (1 - elapsed/window) + current. Tiny memory, error of a few percent (Cloudflare reported about 0.003% wrong decisions in their data).
  4. Token bucket. A bucket holds up to burst tokens and refills at a steady rate; each request takes one. Allows bursts and enforces an average. Stripe and AWS API Gateway use it.
  5. Leaky bucket. Requests go in a queue that drains at a fixed rate; smooths output but adds latency and drops when full. Good for traffic shaping, e.g. NGINX limit_req.

Chosen: token bucket as default (burst-friendly, O(1) memory), sliding window counter where strictness matters (login attempts).

Worked example. Limit 100/min, burst 20: refill rate 100/60 = 1.67 tokens/s, bucket cap 20. A client idle for 12 s has 20 tokens and can send 20 at once, then 1.67/s.

Atomic check in Redis

Two clients checking at once must not both pass. Use one Lua script (Redis runs it atomically, no interleaving):

# KEYS[1]=bucket key; ARGV: rate(tokens/s), capacity, now_ms, cost
LUA = """
local d = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(d[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[2])
local ts = tonumber(d[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
local delta = math.max(0, tonumber(ARGV[3]) - ts) / 1000
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[2]), tokens + delta * tonumber(ARGV[1]))
local allowed = tokens >= tonumber(ARGV[4])
if allowed then tokens = tokens - tonumber(ARGV[4]) end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3])
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], 120000)
return allowed and 1 or 0
"""

Use Redis server time (TIME) or one NTP-synced clock source; mixed client clocks cause drift. PEXPIRE removes idle keys so memory self-cleans.

Scaling and sharding

Redis Cluster hashes the key to 16,384 slots; each user lives on one shard, so a check is a single-shard call. 17,000/s fits one node, but run 3 primaries with 1 replica each for availability and headroom. A hot key (one abusive IP at 100k/s) hammers one shard: add a local pre-filter that blocks it for 1 s after the first deny.

Failure modes and decisions

  • Redis down: fail-open (allow) for normal APIs so an outage does not become a total outage; fail-closed for security-sensitive limits (login, OTP). Make this per-rule. Add a short circuit breaker with 50 ms timeout.
  • Replica lag after failover: counters may reset, allowing a short over-allowance; acceptable.
  • Race between servers is solved by the atomic script; do not do GET then SET.
  • Thundering herd after window reset: add jitter to Retry-After.

Multi-tier and fairness

Layer limits: per-IP (anonymous), per-user, per-endpoint, global protection (total QPS to the DB). Use weights (cost) for heavy calls (search = 5 tokens). Return Retry-After so well-behaved clients back off.

Everyday analogy. A token bucket is a jar of coins that refills slowly; you can spend several at once but cannot spend more than you have.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing the boundary-burst flaw of fixed windows.
  • Choosing sliding log at 10M users.
  • Fail-closed everywhere, so a Redis blip takes the whole API down.
  • Using client wall clocks for refill timing.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Ask what to limit by and what the limit means before designing.
  • Compare at least 3 algorithms with memory and accuracy trade-offs, and pick one with a reason.
  • Know why atomicity matters and show a Lua script or INCR+EXPIRE.
  • Discuss distributed concerns: shared store, sharding, hot keys, clock source.
  • State fail-open vs fail-closed and per-rule exceptions.
  • Mention client behaviour: 429, Retry-After, headers, backoff with jitter.
  • Seniors add local+global layering, config hot reload, observability (allowed/denied rate per rule, p99 limiter latency) and abuse that rotates IPs.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing only the algorithm and never the distributed system around it.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A limiter is a counter per key with a rule, checked at the gateway; 429 plus Retry-After on rejection.
  • Token bucket is the best default (burst plus steady rate, tiny memory); sliding window counter for strict limits; fixed window has a 2x boundary burst.
  • Make the check atomic with a Redis Lua script; shard by key; add a local pre-filter for hot keys.
  • About 17k checks/s and ~1 GB for 10M keys: one small Redis cluster is enough.
  • Fail-open for general APIs, fail-closed for login/OTP; choose per rule.
  • The algorithm is reversible behind an interface, but customers feel behaviour changes, so migrate carefully.

questions.promptHtml: What is the token bucket algorithm, and why is it usually preferred over a fixed window counter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know the basic algorithms and their flaws, not just the name.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at rate r. Each request takes a token; no token means 429. It allows short bursts up to B but enforces the average rate r, and uses O(1) memory. A fixed window counter is simpler, but a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, getting 2x the limit in a short time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Fixed window: INCR key, EXPIRE key 60. Boundary burst: 100 requests at 10:00:59 and 100 at 10:01:00 are all allowed.
  • Token bucket: store (tokens, lastRefillTs). On each request compute tokens = min(B, tokens + elapsed * r), then spend one.
  • Worked example: limit 100/min, burst 20: r = 100/60 = 1.67 tokens/s, cap 20. An idle client has 20 tokens, can send 20 at once, then 1.67/s.
  • Others: sliding log (exact, but O(requests) memory), sliding window counter (weights previous and current window, tiny memory, few percent error), leaky bucket (drains a queue at a fixed rate, smooths output, adds latency).
Refill (rate r) -> Bucket (cap B) -> request takes 1 token

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not knowing the 2x boundary flaw of fixed windows.
  • Computing refill with client wall clocks.
  • Forgetting an idle bucket must be capped at B.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When would you use sliding window counter instead? -> Strict limits like login attempts, where bursts are undesirable.
  2. Why not sliding log at 10M users? -> 100 timestamps x 8 B x 10M = about 8 GB vs about 1 GB for buckets.
  3. How does leaky bucket differ? -> It enforces a smooth output rate with a queue; token bucket permits bursts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer describes the bucket. The senior gives the memory math, the boundary-burst flaw and picks per use case.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fixed-window limiter on a payments API let a partner's retry storm double through at window rollover and overload a downstream service.

questions.promptHtml: You have 20 API gateway servers sharing one Redis for limits. Why can a GET-then-SET token check be wrong, and how do you make it correct and fast?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Atomicity in a shared store is the heart of a distributed limiter.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Two gateways can both read "1 token left" and both spend it, so the limit is exceeded. I run the whole refill, check and decrement as one Redis Lua script; Redis is single-threaded per shard, so scripts do not interleave. That is one round trip per request, key sharded by user so it hits one shard.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The script reads tokens and ts with HMGET, refills based on elapsed time, compares with the cost, subtracts if allowed, writes back with HSET and sets PEXPIRE so idle keys disappear.

LUA = """
local d = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(d[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[2])
local ts = tonumber(d[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
local delta = math.max(0, tonumber(ARGV[3]) - ts) / 1000
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[2]), tokens + delta * tonumber(ARGV[1]))
local allowed = tokens >= tonumber(ARGV[4])
if allowed then tokens = tokens - tonumber(ARGV[4]) end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3])
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], 120000)
return allowed and 1 or 0
"""
  • Time source: use one clock. Redis TIME inside the script or synced NTP; mixed client clocks cause drift.
  • Redis Cluster hashes the key to a slot, so one user lives on one shard.
  • 17k checks/s is far below one node's capacity (100k+ simple ops/s).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Two calls (GET, SET) instead of one script.
  • Using MULTI/EXEC without understanding it does not allow conditional logic on read values.
  • No PEXPIRE, so memory grows forever.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Could you use INCR instead? -> Yes for fixed window or sliding window counters; INCR is atomic by itself.
  2. What if Redis restarts and loses data? -> Buckets refill to full, a short over-allowance; acceptable.
  3. A key spans two shards? -> It should not: use one key per (rule, subject), or hash tags to co-locate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "use Redis". The senior explains why the race exists, shows the Lua script, handles clocks and TTL.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A limiter that did GET then SET let 30% more traffic through at peak because gateways raced on the same keys.

questions.contextHtml:
Tuesday 10:12: the Redis cluster behind the limiter loses its primary and fails over (about 20 s). The API gateways are configured fail-closed everywhere. Metrics:

10:12:05  gateway 5xx rate: 0.1% -> 61%
10:12:05  limiter check timeout (200 ms): 14,800/s
10:12:25  redis failover complete, 5xx rate returns to 0.2% after 40 s

The checkout flow was down for about a minute. The business asks you to make sure this never happens again, but also does not want login brute force to be easier.
questions.promptHtml: What is the right policy and how do you implement it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make Redis never fail" or "fail open everywhere", ignoring login and OTP.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which rules protect security (login, OTP) and which protect capacity? How long is the failover? What is the downstream's real capacity if limits vanish?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Switch the general API rules to fail-open via config; keep login and OTP fail-closed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Limiter as hard dependency with a 200 ms timeout multiplies the outage; no circuit breaker.
  4. How I'd verify each: Gateway logs for limiter timeouts; trace a request and see time spent waiting.
  5. Root cause: An availability dependency on a non-critical safety control with a long timeout and no fallback.
  6. Fix: Per-rule failureMode: open|closed. A 20 to 50 ms timeout and a circuit breaker that trips after N failures. A local in-process limiter as a fallback during Redis outage (approximate, N times the limit at worst).
  7. Prevention: Chaos test that kills Redis primary; alerts on limiter error rate; replicas and a client that follows failover.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pure fail-open lets abusers through for those seconds, acceptable for general APIs; for login I accept some user friction over brute-force risk.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fail-open during an attack? -> Local limiter plus WAF rules at the edge keep a floor.
  • Replica lag after failover resets counters? -> Short over-allowance; acceptable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A limiter timeout of 2 s was left from a prototype; a Redis blip turned into a full-site outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fail-open or fail-closed without nuance.
  • Hire: per-rule policy and short timeout.
  • Strong hire: circuit breaker, local fallback and chaos testing.

questions.contextHtml: A teammate implemented a sliding window log (a Redis sorted set of timestamps) for the public API. 10M active keys, limit 100 requests/min, Redis memory is 41 GB and growing, ZADD/ZREMRANGEBYSCORE CPU is 70%. They say "it is the most accurate".
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate it and propose a cheaper design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Defends accuracy without computing memory; or switches to fixed window ignoring the boundary burst.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How strict must the limit be? Is a few percent error acceptable? Is bursting acceptable for this API?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower the retention (PEXPIRE on keys) and trim aggressively; no change in algorithm yet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Memory is O(requests): 10M keys x 100 timestamps x 8 B is about 8 GB raw, the sorted set overhead (skiplist plus hash) multiplies it several times, matching 41 GB.
  4. How I'd verify each: MEMORY USAGE key, INFO memory, slowlog.
  5. Root cause: An exact algorithm chosen without checking memory at scale.
  6. Fix: Token bucket: about 100 B per key, 10M x 100 B = about 1 GB, one Lua call. For strict endpoints use the sliding window counter: prev x (1 - elapsed/window) + current, two counters per key, error of a few percent.
  7. Prevention: Estimates in the design doc; a memory alert on the limiter cluster.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would keep the exact log only for tiny, security-critical sets (for example, 5 login attempts).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Customers complain about being blocked after a burst? -> Token bucket's burst parameter tuned up.
  • Need exact audit of requests? -> Log events to Kafka, not Redis.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "perfect" limiter used more memory than the product's entire cache; replacing it with buckets freed 40 GB.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: defends the log.
  • Hire: computes memory, proposes bucket or counter.
  • Strong hire: mixes algorithms by rule and explains accuracy error.

questions.contextHtml:
One IP sends 110k requests/s at POST /login. Redis Cluster has 3 primaries; one is at 100% CPU, the others at 15%. Limiter latency p99 went from 1 ms to 90 ms for everyone whose keys live on that shard.

redis-2  cpu 100%  ops 118k/s  slowlog: EVALSHA rl:ip:203.0.113.9:login
redis-1  cpu 14%   ops 17k/s
redis-3  cpu 16%   ops 18k/s
questions.promptHtml: How do you protect the shard and the other users?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds shards; unaware that one key always maps to one shard.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: One IP or many (botnet)? Is the traffic already denied? Do we have a WAF or edge to block at?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the IP at the edge or WAF; add it to a local deny list on gateways.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Single hot key (more shards will not help); legitimate NAT with many users (check headers); retry loop in a client.
  4. How I'd verify each: redis-cli --hotkeys, gateway logs grouped by IP and user agent, ratio of 401s.
  5. Root cause: Each check for the key goes to one shard; every denied request still costs a Redis round trip.
  6. Fix: A local pre-filter: after the first deny, block that key in process memory for about 1 s, so most denied requests never reach Redis. Edge-level blocking for sustained abuse. Per-rule limits for login.
  7. Prevention: Alert on shard skew; two-layer limiter (local approximate, then global).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The local layer lets up to N servers times the limit slip, acceptable for abuse control. I would not block by IP alone for corporate NAT; combine with account-level limits.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Botnet with 100k IPs? -> Per-account and global limits, CAPTCHA, device fingerprinting.
  • Retry-After added? -> Good clients back off; add jitter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A credential stuffing run hammered one shard; the local deny cache cut Redis traffic 95% in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "add Redis nodes".
  • Hire: identifies hot key, local pre-filter, edge block.
  • Strong hire: layers, NAT caveat and account-level limits.

questions.subtopic: Capacity and design for stated scale
questions.contextHtml: Today: 500M API requests/day, average 5.8k/s, peak 17k/s, 10M active keys, one Redis primary with replica handles it with ~12% CPU. Next year a partner program will make it 10x: 170k/s peak, 100M active keys. p99 limiter budget is 2 ms; latency budget on the network is about 0.5 ms intra-region.
questions.promptHtml: Does the design still work? What changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just scale Redis" with no numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are keys per user or per IP? Is the 100M a single region? Do rules need global exactness or is approximate fine?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None; this is planning.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Memory: 100M x 100 B = about 10 GB, fits. Throughput: 170k/s of Lua calls exceeds a single node's comfortable range (100k+ simple ops/s, scripts cost more). Network round trip per request is the latency risk.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test one shard with the real script: measure ops/s and p99 at 50k/s.
  5. Root cause: Not a fault; a threshold crossing.
  6. Fix: Redis Cluster with 6 primaries (about 28k/s each, headroom), keys sharded by subject; keep per-rule hash tags so one check is one shard. Add a local limiter first: it absorbs bursts and obvious abuse. For heavy users use batching of tokens: a gateway leases 10 tokens at a time from Redis and spends locally, cutting calls 10x at the cost of small inaccuracy.
  7. Prevention: Per-shard CPU and p99 dashboards; capacity review each quarter.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the limiter a separate network service for every call unless needed; the extra hop breaks the 2 ms budget.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multi-region with global limits? -> Per-region limits with a sync of counters every second or so; exact global limits cost cross-region latency.
  • A new shard added? -> Slot migration; buckets refill, brief over-allowance.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Token leasing cut a limiter's Redis traffic from 160k/s to 20k/s for the heaviest tenants with under 5% error.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no math.
  • Hire: shows ops and memory math, adds shards.
  • Strong hire: token leasing, local layer, latency budget, multi-region caveats.

questions.contextHtml: Customers currently get a fixed window limit of 1,000/hour. You are moving to a token bucket (rate 1,000/h, burst 100) to stop boundary bursts. Two weeks after the change plan was announced, support is worried: customers have built batch jobs that fire at the top of each hour and rely on getting all 1,000 at once.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate without breaking customers or the system?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Flips the algorithm for everyone on a Monday.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which customers use burst patterns (we can measure)? Is the SLA written in terms of windows? Can the algorithm sit behind an interface?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; plan a shadow phase.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Behaviour change is the risk, not performance. A 100-burst bucket will deny top-of-hour batch jobs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the new algorithm in shadow mode: compute decisions alongside the old, log disagreements, count customers who would be denied.
  5. Root cause: The algorithm's behaviour is part of the customer contract.
  6. Fix: Interface RateLimiter.check(key, cost); shadow mode for two weeks; per-customer rollout flag; for batch customers set a larger burst (for example burst 1,000) or move them to a quota rule; announce early with the new headers (RateLimit-*, Retry-After).
  7. Prevention: Dashboard of would-deny vs allow per customer; kill switch to revert to the old algorithm instantly (it is reversible while both exist).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not switch globally in one step. Big burst values keep part of the boundary flaw, but the cost is bounded because the hourly average is still enforced.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old counters in Redis? -> Use new key names, let old ones expire.
  • A customer disputes a 429? -> Log decision, remaining tokens and rule id per denial.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A change from window to bucket generated a week of support tickets from a partner whose nightly import was now throttled; shadow mode would have predicted it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips it.
  • Hire: shadow mode, gradual rollout.
  • Strong hire: customer-specific burst, kill switch, communication and metrics.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident: a deploy slowed the API; the limiter started returning 429 to many clients. Instead of recovering, load tripled for 15 minutes. Logs:

11:03:00 requests/s 18k   429s/s 1.1k
11:03:30 requests/s 41k   429s/s 24k
11:04:00 requests/s 55k   429s/s 38k   (retry-after header: absent)
client sdk v1.2: retries immediately, up to 5 times, no backoff

The limiter latency stayed at 1 ms; the app servers fell over from the extra connection handling.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident analysis: causes, actions, and what you change in the API contract.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the deploy only, "raise the limits".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What did the clients do with 429s? Do headers exist? Was the limiter itself healthy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Temporarily lower retries via server hints; block the worst SDK version at the edge; return Retry-After immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing Retry-After; client SDK retry without backoff; limiter at the wrong layer (denials still cost app resources).
  4. How I'd verify each: Group requests by client version, count retries per request id, compare 429 rate over time.
  5. Root cause: 429s without guidance created a feedback loop: each denial made the client send up to 5 more requests.
  6. Fix: Always send Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers; fix the SDK (exponential backoff with jitter, honour Retry-After); reject at the gateway before expensive work; put a concurrency limit on app servers.
  7. Prevention: SDK tests for retry behaviour; alert on 429 ratio plus retry ratio; load test with misbehaving clients.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise limits to hide the storm; I would not drop connections silently, which only invites retries.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups

• Clients we do not control? -> Add jitter to Retry-After and edge-level shedding.
  • Cost-based limits? -> A cost per call so heavy endpoints consume more tokens.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A well-meaning SDK retried 429s five times instantly; one flaky minute became a 15-minute outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the deploy.
  • Hire: identifies retry loop and headers.
  • Strong hire: SDK fix, edge shedding, jitter, metrics and contract changes.
